title: Partition employees into those earning above a threshold and those not, and in the same pass count how many fall in each partition, using `Collectors.partitioningBy` with a `counting` downstream. Explain how partitioningBy differs from groupingBy and why it always has exactly two keys.
shortTitle: Partition employees into high and low earners and count each partition using partitioningBy with a downstream collector

s1_definition.profdef: `Collectors.partitioningBy(predicate)` splits a stream into exactly two groups keyed by the boolean `true` and `false`, returning a `Map<Boolean, List<T>>`. The two-argument form adds a downstream collector applied to each partition, for example `partitioningBy(pred, counting())` to count each side.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh sorts salary slips into just two trays: "above ten lakh" and "not above ten lakh". partitioningBy always makes exactly these two trays, even if one ends up empty, and he can count the slips in each tray as he sorts.
s1_definition.oneliner: `partitioningBy(pred)` always yields two keys, true and false; add a downstream collector to reduce each side in the same pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.partitioningBy(predicate)` splits a stream into exactly two groups keyed by the boolean `true` and `false`, returning a `Map<Boolean, List<T>>`. The two-argument form adds a downstream collector applied to each partition, for example `partitioningBy(pred, counting())` to count each side.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh sorts salary slips into just two trays: "above ten lakh" and "not above ten lakh". partitioningBy always makes exactly these two trays, even if one ends up empty, and he can count the slips in each tray as he sorts.

**One line to remember:** `partitioningBy(pred)` always yields two keys, true and false; add a downstream collector to reduce each side in the same pass.

sections.s2_technical:
`partitioningBy(predicate)` is a specialization of grouping where the classifier is a boolean predicate, so the result map always has exactly two keys: `true` for elements that satisfy the predicate and `false` for those that do not. Even if no element falls on one side, that key still exists with an empty collection, which is a guarantee groupingBy does not give.

The two-argument form `partitioningBy(predicate, downstream)` applies a downstream collector to each partition. For counts, `employees.stream().collect(partitioningBy(e -> e.getSalary() > 1_000_000, counting()))` returns `Map<Boolean, Long>` with the count of high earners under true and the rest under false. The downstream can be any collector — toList, counting, averagingDouble, mapping, and so on.

The senior nuance is the difference from groupingBy: groupingBy can produce any number of keys and only creates a key when at least one element maps to it, while partitioningBy is strictly two-valued and always includes both keys. Use partitioningBy when the split is a true/false business rule, because the guaranteed both-keys-present property avoids null-handling when you read the result, and it is slightly more efficient than grouping by a boxed Boolean.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a compliance report that splits employees into high earners, who need enhanced due diligence, and everyone else, and it must show the count on each side. Even if there happen to be zero high earners, the report must still show a zero rather than a missing row.

This is exactly what partitioningBy with a counting downstream does — it always produces both the true and false keys, and counts each partition in a single pass, so the report never has a missing side.

The code defines `Employee`, a `ComplianceReport.countByEarnerClass` method, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five employees with a threshold of one million.

Step 1: partitioningBy evaluates the predicate for each: Rajesh and Sneha exceed the threshold (true), Priya, Amit, and Neha do not (false).

Step 2: The result map is seeded with both keys, true and false, guaranteed present.

Step 3: The counting downstream tallies each partition: two on the true side, three on the false side.

Step 4: Reading counts.get(true) gives 2 and counts.get(false) gives 3, with no risk of a missing key.

```
INFO: High earners (>1M): 2
INFO: Others: 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [Rajesh 1.2M, Sneha 1.5M, Priya 0.9M, Amit 0.7M, Neha 0.65M]
    │ partitioningBy(salary > 1M, counting())
    ▼
  {
    true  = 2   (Rajesh, Sneha)
    false = 3   (Priya, Amit, Neha)
  }
  Both keys ALWAYS present (even if one side is 0)
```

```
  Call chain:
  1. partitioningBy(salary>threshold, counting())
  2. map.get(true) / map.get(false)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
partitioningBy is a specialized grouping where the classifier is a boolean predicate, so the result map always has exactly two keys — true for the elements that satisfy the predicate and false for those that do not. The important guarantee is that both keys are always present, even if one partition is empty, which groupingBy does not promise. The two-argument form adds a downstream collector applied to each side, so with counting I get the size of each partition in one pass.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India a compliance report split employees into high earners, who needed enhanced due diligence, and everyone else, and had to show the count on each side. I used partitioningBy on the salary predicate with a counting downstream, and because both keys are guaranteed I could read the true and false counts directly without worrying about a missing row when a side happened to be empty.

The senior point I always make is to choose partitioningBy over groupingBy specifically when the split is a true/false business rule. groupingBy can produce any number of keys and only creates a key when at least one element maps to it, so you risk a missing key, whereas partitioningBy is strictly two-valued with both keys present. That both-keys guarantee removes null-handling when reading the result and is slightly more efficient than grouping by a boxed Boolean.
